prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Today outside your prison I stand and rattle my walking stick: Prisoners, listen; you have relatives outside. And there are thousands of ways to escape. Years ago I bent my skill to keep my cell locked, had chains smuggled to me in pies, and shouted my plans to jailers; but always new plans occured to me, or the new heavy locks bent hinges off, or some stupid jailer would forget and leave the keys. Inside, I dreamed of constellations— those feeding creatures outlined by stars, their skeletons a darkness between jewels, heroes that exist only where they are not. Thus freedom always came nibbling my thought, just as—often, in light, on the open hills— you can pass an antelope and not know and look back, and then—even before you see— there is something wrong about the grass. And then you see. That’s the way everything in the world is waiting. Now—these few more words, and then I’m gone: Tell everyone just to remember their names, and remind others, later, when we find each other. Tell the little ones to cry and then go to sleep, curled up where they can. And if any of us get lost, if any of us cannot come all the way— remember: there will come a time when all we have said and all we have hoped will be all right. There will be that form in the grass.

Here is a polished, highly eloquent, and professional version of your text that preserves all original meaning, imagery, and poetic metaphors:

***

Today, I stand outside your prison walls, rattling my walking stick against the iron bars. Listen to me, prisoners: you have kin waiting outside, and the paths to freedom are beyond count. 

Years ago, I devoted my own efforts to keeping my cell locked—smuggling chains inside pies and openly declaring my plans to the guards. Yet, fresh ideas continually arose; heavy locks wringed hinges from the walls, or a negligent jailer would leave his keys behind. Inside, I contemplated the constellations—those celestial creatures outlined by stars, their skeletons formed by the void between jewels, heroes defined only by their absence. In this way, freedom persistently nibbled at my thoughts, much like passing an antelope on a bright, open hill without noticing—until you glance back and intuitively sense, even before seeing, that something is subtly altered in the grass. And then, at last, you perceive it. That is how everything in this world lies in wait.

Now, a few final words before I depart: Bid everyone remember their true names, and remind one another when we inevitably reunite. Tell the little ones to shed their tears and then rest, curled up wherever shelter allows. And should any of us lose our way—should any fail to complete the journey—remember this: a time will come when all we have spoken and all we have hoped for will be made right. 

There will be that form waiting in the grass.
outputs.L2:
Currently, I am stationed outside your jail, banging my cane against the ground to draw the inmates' attention. Hear this: your kinfolk await you out here, and the avenues for breaking free are virtually infinite. 

Decades ago, I used all my cunning to ensure my own captivity—having shackles hidden inside pastries delivered to my cell and blurting out my getaway schemes directly to the guards. Yet, despite my efforts, fresh escape ideas kept springing up, heavy padlocks caused the door frames to snap under their weight, or careless guards unwittingly dropped their ring of keys. 

While held captive, my mind wandered to star clusters—grazing beasts defined by points of celestial light, their internal structures formed by dark voids between sparkling gems, legendary champions who are present precisely through their absence. In this exact manner, liberty continuously gnawed at my consciousness. It mirrors walking through sunlit, open fields: you might pass a wild antelope without realizing it, glance back, sense an anomaly in the terrain before your eyes even register it, and then finally make out the animal. That is how the entire universe remains in quiet expectation.

Before taking my leave, I offer these final remarks: Urge every person to hold fast to their individual identity, and make sure they prompt one another of who they are when we eventually reconnect. Instruct the youngsters to shed their tears and then drift off, bedding down in whatever spots they can find. And should any of our group lose their path or fail to complete the journey, keep this truth close: a moment will arrive when every spoken word and cherished wish will be fully restored. That hidden shape will ultimately reveal itself in the meadow.

### A Message of Hope Beyond the Walls

To anyone who currently feels trapped within the shadows of their circumstances, hear this truth first: you are not alone, and your current isolation is not permanent. No matter how restricted your world may seem right now, endless paths toward escape are always present. The horizon of your life is far wider than the immediate constraints that surround you, and a way forward is constantly waiting to be found.

It is essential to understand that all forms of confinement are inherently fragile. Though walls may appear solid and barriers impenetrable, they are built on a flawed foundation. The human impulse toward freedom is a persistent, untamable force that acts like water against rock—constantly seeking, eroding, and creating unexpected fractures in the structures designed to hold it. Because this desire for liberation never stops burning, new opportunities to break free are continuously coming into existence, often in the most surprising of moments.

True freedom, however, rarely arrives with a loud trumpet call. More often, it exists quietly and subtly in the world around us. It lives in the small, overlooked details of our daily lives, waiting patiently for a sudden moment of clarity. Liberation begins with a shift in perception—a sudden realization that the door was unlocked all along, or that the strength to walk away has been within you the entire time. When that spark of discovery lights your path, you must be ready to recognize it and act.

In the meantime, the work of survival requires deep endurance and solidarity. Do not allow your current captivity to erase who you are; preserve your identity, your history, and your core values fiercely. Reach out to comfort the children, shielding them from despair and reminding them of the light ahead. Support one another, lean on your shared strength, and hold fast to one another until the day comes when you can all be reunited in safety and joy. 

Finally, hold onto the assurance that no pain or loss experienced on this journey is final. Though some may be lost along the difficult path to liberation, their presence and courage remain part of the collective whole. Have faith that every shared hope, every whispered prayer, and every broken promise will eventually be redeemed. In the end, all words will be made right, and freedom will have the final say.
outputs.L4:
To all who find themselves bound—whether by the heavy iron of physical walls or the quiet, invisible chains of fear, grief, and circumstance—hear this truth: your current state is not your permanent home. Confinement, in all its bitter forms, seeks first to strip away your humanity, convincing you that the boundary of your world is defined entirely by the boundaries of your cage. 

To survive and ultimately break free, your first act of rebellion must take place within. You must fiercely protect the sanctuary of your core identity. Do not allow the silence of your surroundings to erase your name, your history, or your capacity for love. Hold fast to the essential spark of who you are, for a captive who remembers their true self is a force that no prison can ever truly contain. 

While you endure, keep your eyes sharp and your mind awake. Liberation rarely arrives with the roar of a trumpet; more often, it approaches in subtle, muted tones. It is found in the unexpected shift of a guard’s shadow, the hairline fracture growing in a stone wall, or the sudden, fleeting window of opportunity that reveals itself only to those who are actively watching. Stay vigilant. Be prepared to move when the unseen door swings open, however briefly.

Above all, take comfort in knowing the true nature of the world. Freedom is not an artificial prize that must be constructed from nothing; it is the fundamental, underlying reality of existence. It is the open sky that remains long after the fortress crumbles; it is the natural state waiting patiently just beyond the threshold of your enclosure. Captivity is merely a temporary interruption of a grander, enduring truth.

Let this bring profound peace to your weary spirit: no struggle in the dark is wasted, no quiet tear is forgotten, and no soul is ever hopelessly lost. The architecture of the universe bends inexorably toward restoration. In the final unfolding of things, every broken hope will be mended, every long-suffering heart will be redeemed, and all who have wandered in bondage will finally find their way back to the expansive light of home. Hold fast, keep watch, and do not lose heart—your freedom is already waiting for you.
outputs.L5:
**Today**, the global conversation surrounding criminal justice is undergoing a profound and necessary transformation. For centuries, prisons were built almost exclusively for isolation and retribution—places designed to sever an individual's connection to the outside world. However, modern perspectives are increasingly challenging this traditional paradigm, shifting the focus toward rehabilitation, human dignity, and systemic reform.

Behind concrete walls and iron bars, **prisoners** navigate a complex reality. While incarcerated, they face the loss of liberty, but they also carry the potential for personal growth, education, and redemption. **Today**, access to vocational training, higher education, and mental health resources inside correctional facilities is proving to be one of the most effective ways to reduce recidivism **and** prepare individuals for successful reintegration into society.

True justice requires looking beyond punishment to address the root causes of crime, such as poverty, trauma, **and** systemic inequality. When society chooses to invest in the potential of **prisoners** **today**, it isn't just benefiting the individuals serving time—it is building safer, more compassionate communities for everyone tomorrow. By fostering empathy **and** creating real opportunities for change, we can bridge the gap between justice **and** humanity.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a haunting prose poem about a former prisoner returning to speak to those still trapped inside, touching on memory, freedom, and an antelope hidden in the grass.
counterfactuals.output: I returned to the perimeter when the evening sky was the color of scraped iron, my hands pressed against the cold diamond-mesh of the fence where your shadows gather. You ask me what the world is like beyond the watchtowers, expecting a paradise of sunlight and unfiltered air, but I tell you that freedom is a heavy, quiet room with no walls to catch your falling weight. Out here, memory is a phantom that walks two paces behind me; even now, my feet measure the sidewalk in the five-step rhythm of a cell, and the clanging of a distant car door still freezes the blood in my chest. I came back to give you my breath through the wire, to tell you that the hardest thing is not surviving the iron, but surviving the vastness after the locks are turned. Yesterday, in the waist-high, sun-bleached grass just past the county line, I saw an antelope. It was so still, so completely folded into the amber shadows of the earth, that I only knew it was alive by the trembling of its ribs. It was not hiding from a predator; it was simply holding the entire wild sky inside its chest, waiting for the wind to change, refusing to be seen by anything that might try to name it. That is what I leave with you tonight—not a key, not a promise of soft grass, but the knowledge of that hidden creature. Keep your eyes on the field beyond your windows; learn the patience of the thing that remains buried in the yellow reed, whole and untouched, long before it ever decides to run.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a monologue written in the style of mid-century American parable poetry. An old man stands outside a prison rattling his cane, telling the inmates how hard he tried to stay locked up, how freedom inevitably breaks in like an antelope unnoticed in the hills, and ending with a message of reassurance to children and lost souls.
counterfactuals.output:
Listen to the iron ring. 
*(Clack. Clack. Clack.)*
I bought this cane of dry hill-ash 
for no other reason than to beat against your fence, 
to stand here on the ditch-side of the county line 
and look in at you through the heavy cross-hatch of the shade.

Listen to me, boys. I tried to get in where you are.
Lord knows I tried. I stole the baker’s heavy brass clock 
and sat upon his porch to wait for the sheriff’s car. 
I smashed the tavern glass; I lied under oath; 
I begged the judge to give me thirty years of rust. 
I wanted four corners. I wanted a stone room small enough 
to keep the terrible sky from leaking into my eyes. 
I wanted the comfort of a deadbolt turning in the dark.

I thought if I could only surrender my legs, 
the world would stop demanding that I walk.

But a man cannot hide in a cage, my friends. 
You think those limestone blocks keep out the earth? 
Freedom is a quiet, trespassing thing. 
It does not wait for the warden’s ring of brass keys. 
It breaks in. It comes uninvited, 
like an antelope unnoticed in the sagebrush hills—
a sudden twitch of tan against the scrub, 
moving over the crest before the hunter clears his eyes, 
already inside your garden, already grazing on the frost.

You wake at three in the morning in your narrow bunk, 
and your chest feels light, and your hands are full of wind, 
and you realize the walls have failed again. 
The vastness has come through the mortar. 
The grass has leaped the wire.

So hear an old fool’s noise upon the iron tonight. 
Do not be afraid of the open meadow that is waiting for you. 
And tell the children, when you write your letters home—
tell the little ones who lie awake in their small beds, 
frightened of the dark that stretches out past the barn—
tell them the wildness means no harm. 

Tell the lost souls, the frightened, the ones hiding in small rooms: 
You cannot lock the beauty out. 
It will find you in the cell. 
It will break your iron locks like dry twigs, 
and it will give you back your legs.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem in the style of William Stafford or W.S. Merwin about the subtle, inevitable nature of freedom, constellations, and remembering names.
counterfactuals.output: There is a quiet way the night unfastens itself from the trees, not by force, but by simply letting go of the light. Freedom is like that. It comes while you are looking somewhere else—a sudden, wide space where the fence used to be, though no one ever came to take the wire down. You stand in the driveway, leaning against the cold fender of a car that has stopped humming, and look up into the deep, unwritten dark. The constellations are not staring back; they are merely doing what they have always done, holding their ancient, burning distance, waiting for someone to draw the invisible lines between them again. To remember a name—the name of a forgotten creek, an old friend, or the bright star hanging just above the eastern ridge—is not to capture anything. It is an act of returning. The mouth opens, a few soft syllables drift out into the frosted air, and for a moment you belong to the same silence that keeps the sky together. You realize then that you were never held as tightly as you thought. The latch was always loose, the dark was always open, and every name you ever learned was just a way of forgiving the distance.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Act as a wise, elderly traveler who has escaped a long captivity. Speak a final message of quiet hope to the people still inside the prison, explaining what freedom feels like and asking them to remember who they are.
counterfactuals.output:
*(A scrap of parchment, pressed flat by worn fingers, slipped beneath the heavy iron grate of the lowest cell block just before dawn.)*

Listen close, my friends. Bend your ears to the cold stone one last time. 

My old bones have finally crossed the threshold. The iron gate has swung shut behind me, not to lock me in, but to lock the shadow out. I am writing this by the pale light of the morning star, sitting in the damp grass a mile down the mountain. 

For thirty years, I sat beside you in the dark. I know the sound of your breathing in the night. I know the way the chill seeps into your joints until you believe your very soul is made of frost and rust. I know how the dark tries to convince you that those four walls are the edge of the cosmos.

They are not.

I came here as a traveler, a man who had walked across deserts and sailed upon silver seas, and yet, after ten years in that cell, even *I* began to forget that a world existed beyond the damp mortar. I began to think the world was only six feet wide.

So let me tell you what lies out here, so you may hold it behind your ribs when the guards turn out the torches.

Freedom is not loud, my children. It is not a clash of cymbals or a grand parade. Freedom is quiet. 

It is the cold, sharp air rushing into the very bottom of your lungs without asking anyone’s permission. It is the feeling of earth beneath your feet—earth that yields, earth that smells of sweet rot and fallen leaves, rather than sunless dust. It is the staggering, terrifying expanse of the sky. When you first look up, your head will swim, because there is no ceiling to catch you. There is only blue, stretching out until it touches the edge of the world, and night after night, a billion stars burning just to keep you company.

Out here, the time belongs to you again. The sun rises not because a bell rings, but because it must. You can walk ten paces, or ten miles, and no one will ask you where your feet are going.

They have taken your days. They have taken your strength. But hear an old man’s final plea: *Do not let them take your names.*

You are not the numbers they call at dusk. You are not the mold on the wall or the rust on the chains. You are weavers, farmers, poets, mothers, and dreamers. You are travelers who have been delayed on your journey, nothing more. The men who guard you wear iron, but iron eventually turns to orange dust. You are made of soft flesh and living spirit, and that is a thing that outlasts every fortress ever built by fearful men.

Keep a spark hidden in your chest. Protect it from the draft. Speak your true names to one another in the dark, so you do not forget the sound of them. Remind each other of the color of wheat, the taste of rain, the sound of laughter in a crowded market. 

I am moving on now. My stride is slow, but every step belongs to me. I will walk toward the coast, and when I reach the sea, I will cast a flower into the water for every one of you left inside.

Hold fast. The world is still out here, vast and patient, waiting for you to claim your place in it once more.

I will leave the lamp burning in my heart until we meet beneath the sun.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic, hopeful fable about captivity and nature that concludes with the idea that everything in the world is waiting for us, and that all we have hoped will ultimately be all right.
counterfactuals.output:
In a tower of polished stone, suspended between the floor and the ceiling, hung a bird cage made of spun copper. Within it lived a bird named Orien, whose feathers were the dark indigo of midnight, speckled with tiny stars of white. 

Orien had known only the smooth, cold curve of his perches, the measured drip of water from a porcelain bowl, and the square patch of sky framed by a high, narrow window. He sang, but his songs were short and coiled tightly, like watchsprings winding down in the quiet room. 

He believed the world consisted only of his cage, the stone walls, and the Great Beyond—a pale, shimmering canvas outside the glass where clouds drifted like silent, sleeping beasts. 

Every evening, a wild ivy vine crept an inch higher along the stone ledge outside the glass. On a day when the autumn light turned the sky to melted honey, a stray gust of wind blew a single, golden birch leaf through a crack in the window pane. It tumbled through the air and slipped between the copper bars of Orien’s cage, landing softly at his feet.

Orien pecked at it gently. It smelled of damp earth, rich pine, and something vast and electric that made the skin beneath his feathers prickle. 

"What are you?" Orien whispered to the leaf.

"I am a promise," murmured a low voice from the sill. 

Orien looked up. Sitting on the stone ledge outside was an old, grey owl, her feathers dusted with the silver of twilight. 

"Is it frightening out there?" Orien asked, pressing his chest against the cold wire of his cage. "The room is quiet. The copper does not shake. Out there, the air moves without walls. How do you keep from falling forever?"

The owl folded her wings, her golden eyes wide and ancient. "You do not fall when you are part of the sky, little star. You are carried. You think yourself safe in your smallness, but you are only waiting. The cage is not your home; it is merely the shell before the hatching."

"Waiting for what?" Orien asked, his heart beating like a tiny drum.

"For your courage to match your wings," the owl replied softly. "Nature does not forget what she has made. Every tree has grown a branch with your name written upon it. Every breeze has saved a breath to lift you."

That night, a storm swept through the valley. It was not an angry storm, but a magnificent, surging chorus of rain and wind. The old wooden frame of the high window groaned, surrendered, and swung wide open. The wind rushed into the stone tower, smelling of ozone, moss, and freedom. It struck the copper cage, and with a soft, rusted click, the latch gave way.

The door swung open.

Orien froze. The cage was open, but the world felt terrifyingly boundless. The air outside was dark and roaring, filled with the shadows of tossing branches and the scent of rain. He clung to his perch, his toes white with strain. To leave was to lose everything he knew, even if all he knew was a cage.

Then, he looked beyond the sill. 

In the heart of the storm, he did not see destruction; he saw movement. He saw the ivy dancing against the stone, intoxicated by the rain. He saw the dark, rolling hills stretching into infinity, alive and breathing. The earth was not a void waiting to swallow him; it was an ocean waiting to hold him up.

Orien took a breath—a deep, full breath that reached the very tips of his midnight wings. He let go of the copper perch. 

He hopped to the threshold of the cage. Then to the stone window ledge. 

The wind caught beneath his feathers, cool and intoxicating. Orien spread his wings for the very first time. He did not drop. The air gathered beneath him like a warm, rushing hand, and with a single beat of his wings, he swept out into the dark, rain-washed night.

He flew. 

He flew over the bowing tops of the pines, through clouds that tasted of sweet water, beneath a moon that unveiled itself just for him, painting the earth in silver and green. He felt the wild, rhythmic pulse of the world, and for the first time, his song burst forth—uncoiled, endless, and triumphant.

He realized then that the wild had never been hostile, nor had it ever forgotten him. The forest had been growing, the rivers had been running, and the winds had been gathering, all preparing for the moment he would join the dance.

And as the storm cleared, revealing the first soft pink ribbons of dawn, Orien landed upon the highest branch of an ancient oak. Warm light washed over his wet feathers, and he knew, with absolute certainty, that the darkness had only been a shadow passing by. 

For he saw now that the sky does not end, that nature holds a place for every living heart, that everything in the world is waiting for us, and that all we have hoped will ultimately be all right.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
